query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning-driven workflow that assimilates partial high-temperature calorimetric and dilatometric data with existing CALPHAD and computational thermodynamic databases can accurately predict the melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloy compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the solid state, composed of five or more principal elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, exhibiting complex atomic interactions and local lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Implementation of a data-driven machine learning model (using a Bayesian or active-learning framework) that integrates sparse high-temperature experimental measurements with extensive computational thermodynamic data and compositional descriptors (e.g., atomic radius mismatch, melting points, enthalpies of mixing).
generation.conditions: Measurements in the solid-to-liquid transition region (near and above the melting point) for HEAs covering a wide compositional space, where the experimental data are limited and traditional methods (e.g., high-temperature DSC, drop calorimetry) are costly and time-consuming.
generation.structural_mediator: The machine learning model, which mediates predictions through physicochemical descriptors and iterative refinement, establishing statistical correlations between partial experimental inputs and computed thermodynamic behavior.
generation.mechanism: By continuously updating its training set with targeted high-temperature calorimetry and dilatometry results, the ML model refines its predictive correlations with thermodynamic databases (such as those used in CALPHAD). This integrated approach leverages both experimental trends and computational predictions to interpolate and potentially extrapolate melting behaviors and fusion-related properties across a wide range of HEA compositions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model is expected to predict melting temperatures with an error margin below 5%, and similarly bounded errors for enthalpy/entropy of fusion and volume changes at melting relative to direct measurements, thus providing reliable estimates for guiding experimental alloy development.
generation.baseline: Traditional high-temperature experimental measurements and standalone CALPHAD predictions, which are limited by extensive resource needs and incomplete thermodynamic data, respectively.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable primarily to HEAs (multi-principal element alloys) with compositions within the established ranges of the training data. Its performance in systems with very non-equiatomic ratios, significant phase segregation, or poorly characterized thermodynamic parameters remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The accuracy and generalizability of the model depend on the quality and quantity of high-temperature experimental data and the completeness of the underlying thermodynamic databases. Prediction uncertainties may increase for novel or poorly sampled regions of the compositional space.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of previously uncharacterized HEA compositions spanning the expected range of the training data. Use the machine learning workflow to predict their melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change at melting. Synthesize these alloys and conduct high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and dilatometry experiments to measure the respective properties.
measurements: Enthalpy and entropy of fusion via calorimetric analysis
Volume change at melting via dilatometry or high-temperature imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimentally measured values for the predicted properties deviate consistently by more than the established uncertainty bounds (e.g., >10% error relative to predictions) across multiple compositions, the validity of the machine learning workflow as a reliable predictive tool will be ruled out.

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: Although the high-entropy alloy field has expanded quickly with progress in mechanical property measurements, most studies have not focused on a broadly applicable, accurate, and efficient determination of fusion-related thermophysical properties and liquid-phase behavior across multiple-principal-element compositions. The one relevant study (PMC8282813) used high-throughput computational screening to identify prospective high-temperature alloys by estimating melting temperatures in the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti system. However, direct, comprehensive determination of melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting for diverse HEA compositions remains underexplored. Models and screening approaches often face limited or incomplete thermodynamic data for these complex alloys, reducing predictive reliability for the liquid phase and phase transformation thermodynamics.
decision.unsolved: High-temperature calorimetric measurements are expensive and challenging, while first-principles or CALPHAD-based computational methods can be hampered by incomplete or uncertain thermodynamic databases for novel HEA compositions. A robust framework that efficiently obtains melting thermodynamics and reliably covers both near-eutectic and off-stoichiometric compositions is missing, especially for large, unexplored regions of composition space.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning-driven workflow that assimilates partial experimental data (e.g., from targeted high-temperature calorimetry and dilatometry) with existing computational databases, then iteratively refines predictive models for melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase properties. Key parameters include thermophysical descriptors (atomic radius mismatch, melting points of constituent elements, enthalpies of mixing, etc.) and carefully curated experimental data used in a Bayesian or active-learning framework.
decision.why: A data-driven approach is the logical progression from current high-throughput computational screening methods (as in PMC8282813) and available calorimetry/CALPHAD data. By systematically incorporating a breadth of partial measurements and compositional descriptors to train machine-learning models, one can rapidly identify correlations and refine predictions over large composition ranges. A decisive validation would involve targeted experimental measurements across multiple new multi-component alloys, directly comparing predicted and measured melting behavior, enthalpies, and densities—if these differ significantly from the ML predictions beyond established uncertainty margins, the approach would be invalidated.
